page.title: Identify a find
page.lead: Photograph it, then compare the closest matches with their dangerous look-alikes.
page.seoDescription: Identify wild mushrooms and plants from a photo, on your own device. Compare the closest matches with their toxic look-alikes.

coverage.note: Across verified records in Europe and the US.

guide.title: For a good match
guide.top: Top and cap: the whole specimen, filling the frame.
guide.under: Underside or stem base: gills, pores or ridges, or the base of the stem, where look-alikes differ.
guide.disagree: Matches disagree? Start over with a cut through the middle as the second photo.

disclaimer.aboveResults: These are possible matches, not a confirmed identification. A dangerous look-alike can be correct even when it is not the top result.
disclaimer.neverEat: Do not eat anything based on this app. A misidentification can be fatal. This tool never confirms that something is safe to eat.

results.heading: Possible matches
results.toxicBanner: One of these matches is toxic. Read every row before going further.
results.notInCatalog: Not in this app's catalog - no safety information
results.cautionGenus: Not in this app's catalog - its genus includes toxic species

mechanisms.amatoxin: Contains amatoxins - the same toxin group as the death cap. Poisoning is often delayed by 6-24 hours, feels like recovery, then causes liver failure. Frequently fatal.
mechanisms.gyromitrin: Contains gyromitrin, which the body converts to a toxin damaging the liver and nervous system. Can be fatal, and is not reliably destroyed by cooking.
mechanisms.muscarine: Contains high levels of muscarine, causing rapid sweating, salivation and collapse. Deaths have been recorded.
mechanisms.orellanine: Contains orellanine, which destroys the kidneys. Symptoms can take days to weeks to appear, long after the meal is forgotten.
mechanisms.isoxazole: Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, causing confusion, nausea and delirium. Rarely fatal but seriously unpleasant.
mechanisms.giIrritant: Causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea, sometimes for days. Not usually fatal, but dehydration can be dangerous.
mechanisms.colchicine: Contains colchicine. There is no antidote, symptoms are delayed, and a small amount can kill an adult.
mechanisms.cardiacGlycoside: Contains cardiac glycosides that disturb the heart rhythm. Can be fatal.
mechanisms.calciumOxalate: Contains needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that burn and swell the mouth and throat.
mechanisms.coniine: Contains coniine, the poison in hemlock. It paralyses the muscles used for breathing. Very small amounts are fatal.
mechanisms.tropane: Contains tropane alkaloids. A handful of berries can kill a child. Sweet taste offers no warning.
mechanisms.poorEdibility: Not dangerous, but poor eating and easily mistaken for something better.
mechanisms.bitter: Not poisonous, but so bitter that a single specimen ruins a whole dish.
mechanisms.taxine: Contains taxine alkaloids, which stop the heart. All parts except the red flesh of the aril are lethal, including the seed inside it. There is no home preparation that makes it safe.
mechanisms.immuneHaemolysis: Triggers an immune reaction that destroys red blood cells. It builds up over repeated meals, so having eaten it before safely is no reassurance at all - the poisoning can arrive after years of eating it.
mechanisms.nephrotoxic: Destroys the kidneys days after the meal, often needing dialysis. Cooking does not help.
mechanisms.rhabdomyolysis: Breaks down muscle tissue after repeated meals, which can stop the heart. Deaths are documented in people who had eaten it for years.
mechanisms.encephalopathy: Causes fatal brain inflammation, especially where kidney function is reduced. It caused a cluster of deaths in Japan among foragers who had eaten it safely before.
mechanisms.aconitine: One of the most toxic plants in Europe. Aconitine stops the heart, poisoning has followed skin contact alone, and there is no antidote.
mechanisms.cicutoxin: Causes violent seizures within an hour and is frequently fatal. A single root is enough. It is among the most poisonous plants in Europe.
mechanisms.ricin: The seeds contain one of the most lethal natural poisons known. A few chewed seeds can kill an adult, and there is no antidote.
mechanisms.cytisine: All parts, especially the seed pods, contain cytisine. Children have died after eating the pods, having taken them for peas.
mechanisms.grayanotoxin: Leaves, flowers and nectar contain grayanotoxins, which disturb heart rhythm. Honey made from the flowers has poisoned people.
mechanisms.veratrumAlkaloid: Collapses blood pressure and heart rate within hours. The young leaves are repeatedly mistaken for wild garlic, and those confusions have been fatal.
mechanisms.coprine: Contains coprine, which stops the body breaking down alcohol. Alcohol drunk in the hours before the meal or up to three days after it causes flushing, a racing heart, nausea and vomiting.
mechanisms.ptaquiloside: Contains ptaquiloside, which causes cancer (bracken is rated possibly carcinogenic to humans), and an enzyme that destroys vitamin B1. Cooking lowers the toxin but does not remove it.
mechanisms.phototoxic: Its sap burns skin in sunlight: painful blisters and scars that can last for years. Do not touch it with bare skin, and keep it away from the eyes.
mechanisms.atractyloside: Contains atractyloside, which shuts down the liver and kidneys. It has killed people who mistook it for wild artichoke or chewed its root.

checks.volva: Look at the very base of the stem, below ground level: a sac-like bag or swollen cup there is a serious warning sign.
checks.gillColour: Gill colour, including on older specimens - pure white gills on a stemmed mushroom deserve caution.
checks.gillAttachment: Whether the underside has true blade-like gills that can be separated with a fingernail.
checks.gillVsRidges: True chanterelles have blunt, forking ridges running down the stem, not thin crowded gills.
checks.sporePrint: Take a spore print: leave the cap gill-side down on paper for a few hours and check the colour.
checks.ringAndStem: Whether there is a ring on the stem, whether it slides freely, and any pattern on the stem below it.
checks.overallSize: Full-grown size. Some deadly look-alikes are much smaller than the edible species they resemble.
checks.capWarts: Whether the cap has removable patches or warts, which can wash off in rain.
checks.cortina: Any cobweb-like veil between cap edge and stem on young specimens, and rusty-brown traces where it was.
checks.capStructure: Whether the head is a regular pitted honeycomb or an irregular brain-like set of folds.
checks.capAttachment: Whether the cap is attached to the stem along its length or hangs free from the top only.
checks.hollowStem: Cut the specimen in half lengthways and check whether it is completely hollow inside.
checks.poreColour: Colour of the pores under the cap, especially any red or orange tones.
checks.fleshBruising: Whether cut or bruised flesh changes colour, and to what.
checks.fleshReddening: Whether the flesh reddens where handled or damaged.
checks.stemNetwork: Any raised net-like pattern on the stem, and its colour.
checks.smell: Crush a leaf or piece and smell it. Wild garlic smells strongly of garlic; its deadly look-alikes do not.
checks.smellCompare: Smell a crushed leaf or the freshly cut flesh and compare it with the edible species: an unexpected or unpleasant smell is a warning sign.
checks.leafArrangement: How leaves emerge: singly from the base on their own stalk, or paired and sheathed together.
checks.leafShape: Leaf outline and veining, including whether the base is arrow-shaped.
checks.stemMarkings: Whether the stem is hollow, ridged, or blotched with purple - and whether it smells unpleasant when crushed.
checks.berryArrangement: Whether berry clusters droop below the branches or stand upright above the foliage.
checks.plantHabit: Whether the plant is a woody shrub or a soft green herb dying back each year.
checks.interiorPattern: Look at the skin and cut it in half. A black truffle has a black skin of small pyramid-shaped warts and a dark inside laced with fine white veins, with a strong, pleasant smell. An earthball has a yellowish to brown, cracked or scaly skin, a thick rind and a purple-black inside, and smells sharp and unpleasant.
checks.berryColour: Ripe berry colour: elderberries for eating are purple-black. Red berries in upright, dome-shaped clusters are red elder, poisonous raw.
checks.flowerShape: Flower shape: violets have five uneven petals with a spur at the back; lesser celandine has 8–12 glossy yellow petals.
checks.latexColour: Break a gill or the cap edge and watch the milk that appears. Saffron milk caps bleed carrot-orange to wine-red milk; white or yellowing milk means another milk cap.
checks.capMargin: Whether the cap edge is rolled under and fringed with long, woolly hairs.
checks.capScales: Whether the cap is covered in shaggy, upturned white scales, or is smooth, grey-brown and finely grooved.
checks.fernStem: Look at the young stem. Ostrich fern fiddleheads are smooth, with brown papery scales and a deep U-shaped groove along the inside of the stem. Bracken is fuzzy, with a round stem and a top that branches in three.
checks.berryBloom: Sloes grow singly on thorny blackthorn and have a dusty blue bloom that rubs off. Buckthorn berries are shiny black, in clusters along the twigs, with no bloom.
checks.jackOLantern: Colour and growth: oysters are grey, brown or cream and grow in shelves on dead wood, with no stem or a short one at the side. The jack-o'-lantern is bright orange through and through, grows in tufts with a real central stem, often at the base of oak or olive trees, and its gills run down that stem.
checks.angelWing: Thickness, colour and wood: angel wings are pure white, thin and fragile, and grow on rotting conifer wood. Oysters are thicker and fleshier, grey, brown or cream, and mostly grow on broadleaf wood.
checks.puffballInterior: Cut it in half from top to bottom. A giant puffball is pure white and soft all through, like marshmallow, with no outline of a cap, gills or stem inside. An earthball has a thick, scaly, yellowish skin and darkens to purple-black inside from the centre, marbled white while young.
checks.sulphurTuft: Colour, stem and spore print: sulphur tuft is sulphur-yellow and grows in dense tufts with real stems; its gills are greenish-yellow, turning purple-black, and its spore print is purple-brown. Oysters are grey, brown or cream, almost stemless, with white to cream gills and a white to pale lilac spore print.
checks.jackOLanternChicken: Underside: chicken of the woods has no gills, only tiny pores on a sulphur-yellow underside, and grows in overlapping brackets on trunks and stumps. The jack-o'-lantern has true orange gills running down a real stem and grows in tufts at the base of trees.
checks.scalyVase: Shape and cap: the scaly vase chanterelle is a tall trumpet, hollow down the middle, with coarse orange-red scales on top. Golden and Pacific chanterelles have a smooth, solid cap with no scales and no deep hollow.
checks.scaberStem: Stem: aspen boletes have a stem covered in rough dark scales (scabers) and an orange cap, and their flesh darkens when cut. King boletes have a smooth stem with a fine pale net and flesh that stays white.
checks.chestnutHusk: Husk and nut: sweet chestnuts sit in a husk covered in dense, fine, needle-sharp spines, usually two or three flat-sided nuts with a pointed tuft at the tip, under long single toothed leaves. Horse chestnuts have a thick husk with a few short, blunt spikes and one or two round, glossy conkers with no point, under leaves shaped like a hand.
checks.hedgeBerries: Where the red fruit hangs: rose hips sit at the ends of thorny, woody stems, each with the dried remains of the flower on top. Black and white bryony and bittersweet are soft climbers twining through the hedge, with bunches of small shiny berries and no thorns.
checks.asparagusShoot: The shoot: wild asparagus shoots rise straight from the ground beside last year's spiny, needle-leaved plant, with small triangular scales pressed against the stem. Bryony shoots twine from the start and carry broad leaves or curling tendrils.
checks.hogweed: Size and stem: giant hogweed grows 2 to 5 m tall, with a thick stem blotched purple and covered in coarse bristles, huge sharply cut leaves and flower heads up to 50 cm across. Elder is a woody shrub; masterwort is knee- to waist-high with broad leaflets in threes. Do not touch hogweed with bare skin.
checks.pimpernel: Stem and flowers: scarlet pimpernel has square, hairless stems, leaves with black dots underneath and small orange-red or blue flowers. Chickweed has round stems with a single line of hairs and small white star flowers with deeply split petals.
checks.spurgeSap: Break a stem: spurges bleed a white, milky sap that burns skin and eyes, and carry small green cup-shaped flowers. Chickweed never has milky sap and has white star flowers.
checks.nightshadeFlower: Flowers and fruit: black nightshade has small white star flowers with a yellow cone in the middle and green berries turning black. Amaranth has no petals at all, only dense spikes of tiny green or reddish flowers.
checks.thornApple: Leaves, flowers and fruit: thorn apple has big, coarsely toothed leaves with an unpleasant smell, large white or violet trumpet flowers and spiny seed capsules. Amaranth leaves are smooth-edged ovals and its flowers are dense spikes with no petals.
checks.thistleRosette: Stem and flower: wild artichoke grows a tall, leafy stem with big purple flower heads. Never eat a stemless thistle rosette or a thistle root: the deadly Chamaeleon gummifer (Atractylis gummifera) flowers flat in the middle of its rosette and has a thick root with a sticky white latex.
checks.arumLeaf: Leaf and veins: lords-and-ladies has large, glossy, arrow-shaped leaves with a net of veins, often dark-spotted, and a hooded flower spike in spring. Sorrel leaves are smaller and matt with sharp backward-pointing lobes; violet leaves are heart-shaped with scalloped edges. Never taste a leaf to check.
checks.plantainVeins: Leaf veins: plantain leaves have five to nine parallel veins that pull out as strings when you tear the leaf, and they are smooth to slightly hairy. Foxglove leaves are soft and downy, with a net of veins, toothed edges and a winged stalk.

critical.lepiotaMacrolepiota: Deadly Lepiota species are among the most dangerous look-alikes for the Parasol mushroom, and this was the single most frequent mistake in our testing. A true Parasol is large, with a movable ring and a snakeskin-patterned stem. Small specimens with a plain stem should be left alone even if they look right.
critical.trufflePair: Both a truffle and a poisonous false truffle are among the matches. From the outside they are genuinely hard to tell apart. Cut the find open before anything else: marbled pale veins mean truffle, a solid dark interior means false truffle.
critical.angelWingPair: Both an oyster mushroom and the angel wing are among the matches. The angel wing has caused fatal brain inflammation. It is thinner, pure white, and grows on conifer wood: check the wood and the flesh thickness before anything else.
critical.veratrumPair: Both wild garlic and white hellebore are among the matches. This confusion has killed people. Crush a leaf: wild garlic smells strongly of garlic, hellebore does not. Hellebore leaves are also strongly ribbed and grow alternately up the stem.
critical.inkCapAlcohol: Both a shaggy mane and the common ink cap are among the matches. The common ink cap reacts violently with alcohol, even alcohol drunk days after the meal. A shaggy mane is tall, white and covered in shaggy scales; the common ink cap is smaller, grey-brown and smooth. If in doubt, leave it, and never drink alcohol with ink caps.
critical.matsutakeSmithiana: Both a matsutake and Amanita smithiana are among the matches. Amanita smithiana destroys the kidneys and has been picked for matsutake in the Pacific Northwest. Smell it and dig out the whole base: a matsutake smells spicy, like cinnamon. Amanita smithiana does not, and its base swells and then tapers into the soil like a root, ringed with white scraps of veil.
critical.puffballPair: Both a giant puffball and a poisonous look-alike are among the matches. Cut it in half from top to bottom before anything else. A puffball is pure white and even all the way through. A purple-black interior means an earthball; the outline of a cap, gills and stem means a young Amanita, which can be deadly.
critical.rampsPair: Both ramps and a poisonous look-alike are among the matches. Lily of the valley, false hellebore and autumn crocus have similar leaves, and all three are toxic. Crush a leaf: ramps smell strongly of onion or garlic, the look-alikes do not. Lily of the valley has two leaves wrapped around one stalk; false hellebore leaves are deeply pleated and climb a stout stem.
critical.fiddleheadBracken: Both ostrich fern fiddleheads and bracken are among the matches. Bracken causes cancer and is not a fiddlehead to eat. Ostrich fern fiddleheads are smooth, with brown papery scales and a deep U-shaped groove inside the stem; bracken is fuzzy and branches in three at the top.
